h: What “linguistically accessible” means for an item
t: Same standard, same cognitive demand, same key. Only the language load changes. Shorter sentences, active voice, familiar words outside the tested vocabulary, no idioms. h: What the test is · Qué es el examen
t: English The ELPT measures how well your child can use English for school — not math, not science, and not how smart they are. Every student who is identified as an English learner (EL) takes it once a year, usually in March to mid-April (2027 window: March 1 – April 16), on a computer, at school, during the school day. It takes about 2–3 hours spread over several days. There is nothing to study for; it is a photograph of where your child's English is right now. p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: How a second language is actually acquired
t: Five findings from second language acquisition research, and what each one asks you to do differently on Monday. Most of what slows an English learner down in a content classroom is not ability, and it is not effort. It is a mismatch between how we teach language and how language is learned. These five findings have held up across decades of research, and every one of them has a move attached. 1

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Language is acquired through understanding, not repetition
t: Students acquire English when they understand messages slightly beyond their current level — what Krashen called comprehensible input. Drills and word lists produce recall; understood language produces acquisition. Your move: keep the content the same and make the message reachable — visuals, gestures, examples, a slower rate with normal vocabulary. Never lower the concept to lower the language. 2

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Silence is a stage, not refusal
t: Newcomers often go through a silent period, absorbing far more than they produce. A student who won't speak in week three may be building the system they'll use in week twelve. Your move: let them show understanding without talking — point, sort, match, draw, thumbs up. Invite speech; don't force it in front of thirty peers. 3

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: The affective filter is real: when students are embarrassed or afraid of being wrong, input stops getting through. Cold calls and public error correction raise that filter fastest. Your move: rehearse answers in pairs before anyone speaks publicly, and respond to meaning first. Learn to pronounce their name correctly — it matters more than any strategy on this page. 4

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Output is where the gaps show up
t: Swain's work on pushed output holds that producing language forces students to notice what they can't yet say. Comprehension alone will not carry a student to Level 4. Your move: every period, require one extended spoken or written response with a frame to support it. A comprehension check is not output. 5

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: What they know in Spanish transfers to English
t: Cummins' work on transfer holds that concepts and literacy skills cross languages — the idea does not have to be relearned, only relabeled. Your move: let students think, discuss, and pre-write in Spanish on the way to English, and point out cognates — analyze / analizar , evidence / evidencia , hypothesis / hipótesis . 1–3 vs. 5–7 Years to fluency Conversational ease arrives first; the academic language of analysis and argument takes far longer. p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Post a content objective and a language objective for every lesson, and say both out loud. Students should be able to tell a visitor what they're learning and how they'll use language to show it. 2

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Connect explicitly to what students already know — including schooling from another country — and pre-teach the three key terms the lesson depends on. 3

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Match your rate to proficiency, define academic terms in the moment, and demonstrate every task before assigning it. Model, then release. 4

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Teach students how to learn: previewing, chunking, note-taking frames, self-questioning. Scaffold with think-alouds and questions that ask for reasoning, not recall. 5

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Structure frequent talk about content in pairs and triads, with grouping that changes by task. Aim to talk less than your students do, and allow home-language clarification. 6

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Give students something to handle, build, sort, or produce that uses all four domains. New vocabulary sticks when it's used, not when it's copied. 7

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
t: Keep both objectives visibly supported all period, hold engagement high, and pace to the students in front of you rather than the plan on paper. 8

t: Close by reviewing key vocabulary and concepts, give feedback on language and content separately, and check comprehension of all students before they leave. Keep the thinking hard and the language reachable. Scaffolding is not lowering the bar — it's building the stairs.

h: Four to seven years, even in strong programs
t: Long-term studies of academic achievement consistently put full academic English proficiency several years out, well past the point where a student sounds fluent. Program quality shortens the timeline; nothing eliminates it. p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Comprehension needs about 95 to 98 percent known words
t: Below that threshold, unknown vocabulary crowds out meaning and students cannot guess their way through a passage. Words also need many encounters in context before they stick — one exposure on a list is not one of them. In your room: pre-teach the few words that carry the passage, then recycle them deliberately in your talk, your questions, and the exit ticket. Long, Gass Interaction and negotiation

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Acquisition accelerates when meaning gets negotiated
t: Input matters most when learners have to work at it with someone — clarifying, confirming, rephrasing. That back-and-forth makes language comprehensible and simultaneously pushes production. In your room: build in structured pair tasks where partners must ask each other something to finish the work, rather than round-robin answers to you. Lyster & Ranta Corrective feedback

p: The Language Bridge — Laurel High School, September 2026
h: Recasts feel kind, prompts get repair
t: Their classroom analysis found recasts to be the most common form of feedback and among the least likely to be noticed as correction, while prompts — clarification requests, elicitation, repetition of the error point — produced far more student self-repair. In your room: keep recasting for flow, but when accuracy matters, pause and elicit: "Say that again with the past tense." Let the student make the fix. Want the citations? h: The first ten days with a young newcomer.
t: Kindergarten through grade 5, in two bands. What to get right each day, how to set up the room, what transfers from the home language, and the printables you need on the desk tomorrow. Written for the classroom teacher; the EL teacher can hand it over as is. K–2 Grades 3–5 Day-by-day Printables English · Español Kindergarten – Grade 2 Grades 3 – 5 Printables

A five- or six-year-old newcomer is not behind. They are learning to read the room before they read the page. The job of the first two weeks is safety, routine, and a hundred words they can use. Day The one thing to get right What the child does What you hand the family 1 A name they hear said correctly, a seat next to a kind buddy, and a bathroom signal. Draws a picture of their family. Learns “bathroom,” “water,” “help,” “yes,” “no.” Your Guide to School in the U.S. in their language. 2 The picture schedule on their desk. Point to it at every transition. Matches schedule cards to the class r

Picture schedule card set (in Printables). Labels with pictures on door, sink, cubbies, materials. A visual “I need…” card on the desk: bathroom, water, help, nurse, I don't understand. Buddy chosen for kindness, not language. Books in the home language, even two, in the class library. Language that works at 5–7

Same short phrases every day: “Line up.” “Eyes on me.” “Show me.” Gesture every time. Songs and chants carry grammar for free; use the ones the class already sings. Total physical response: say it, do it, have them do it. Accept one word or a point as an answer for weeks. Then ask for two words. Reading and math

Spanish, Portuguese, Vietnamese: the alphabet transfers; teach the sounds that differ (short vowels, th, sh). Arabic, Chinese: teach letter shapes with sand, body movement, tracing. Math: numbers and operations transfer almost completely; the word problem is the barrier, not the math. Pair every number with the quantity (dots, cubes) for the first month.

h: The four lanes, for little ones
t: Newcomer Weeks 1–8 for most Points, matches, sorts, draws, copies. Says single words and memorized chunks. Needs a buddy and pictures for everything. Emerging Often by mid-year Two- and three-word phrases. Follows routine directions without the gesture. Starts to retell with picture support. Progressing Year two for many Simple sentences about what they see and do. Reads decodable text. Needs vocabulary pre-taught for content. Challenge Near grade-level peers Push for complete sentences, past tense, “because.” Give them the job of explaining to the next newcomer.

A nine-year-old newcomer is old enough to be embarrassed and young enough to catch up fast. They often read and compute at or above grade level in their first language. Protect their dignity and give them content from day one. Day The one thing to get right What the student does What you hand the family 1 A private tour, a buddy who shares a language if possible, and a way to say “I don't understand” without an audience. Fills in an “All about me” page with pictures and home-language writing allowed. Learns the five survival phrases. Your Guide to School in the U.S. ; ask what the student stud

No kindergarten books in front of peers. Use high-interest, low-text books, graphic novels, and bilingual texts. Group them with strong, kind readers, not with the lowest group. Let them show what they know in the home language on paper; you can get it translated. Content from day one

h: Lower the language, not the thinking
t: Every lesson: five words with pictures, one sentence frame, one diagram. Use EL Bridge with the K–12 ELA, math, or science standard; the Newcomer lane is written for exactly this. Accept labeled drawings and single-sentence answers as evidence for a month. Reading transfer

h: Readers in one language become readers in two
t: Find out if they read in the home language. If yes, comprehension strategies transfer; teach English sounds and vocabulary. If no, this is a reading-instruction need, not an English need; loop in the reading interventionist. Cognates for Spanish speakers: 30–40% of academic English. Make a cognate wall.

Newcomer Semester one for most Labels, matches, copies sentence frames. Math computation at grade level with the problem read aloud. Emerging Often by spring Short sentences with a frame; reads picture-supported text; retells with a sequence organizer. Progressing Year two Paragraphs with a frame that fades; grade-level text with glossed words; participates in group work with a role. Challenge Near exit Grade-level tasks; coach academic vocabulary and connectors. Give them a leadership role in groups.
